Momentum is central to stochastic optimization in deep learning, including the training of large language models. Classical momentum methods typically rely on a fast exponential moving average (EMA) scheme, which discounts past gradients on a fixed timescale and may underweight older gradients that remain informative. This creates a trade-off between retaining long-term history and adapting to recent changes. We introduce Hybrid Momentum ( HyM ), which combines a linearly weighted average of past gradients with a geometrically discounted fast momentum. The former assigns weights proportional to the gradients’ iteration indices and retains a growing span of history, while the latter emphasizes recent gradients. This hybrid construction is modular and can be combined with adaptive preconditioning and other update transformations. In particular, we propose HyMUON , which applies Newton–Schulz orthogonalization to the hybrid direction. Illustrative examples and controlled experiments demonstrate the benefits of combining gradient information across these two timescales. Across image classification, machine translation, and language modeling, HyM and HyMUON match or improve upon strong baselines. HyMUON improves over Muon on IWSLT14, and in both the 100k- and 600k-step GPT-2 124M OpenWebText regimes. For LLaMA-1.3B pretraining on C4, HyMUON achieves a final validation loss of 2.777 2.777 , compared with 2.903 2.903 for Muon.

Momentum methods improve stochastic optimization by combining the current gradient with information from earlier updates. In deep learning, this history is usually maintained through exponential moving averaging (EMA), which assigns geometrically decaying weights to past gradients, as in Heavy-Ball momentum and commonly used Nesterov updates ( Polyak, 1964 ; Sutskever et al., 2013 ) . EMA emphasizes recent gradients while strongly reducing the influence of older gradients on subsequent updates. When gradient contributions that reduce a particular target loss occur intermittently across mini-batches, retaining a longer history may help accumulate these contributions. By combining momentum with iterate averaging, Defazio et al. (2024) proposed the Schedule-Free method, which achieves strong empirical performance without a prescribed schedule for learning rate decay. The empirical success of Schedule-Free optimization motivates revisiting how this history is accumulated. In this form, the update combines a running weighted sum of past gradients with the current gradient. As training proceeds, this weighted sum spans a longer history, but each new gradient contributes a smaller fraction of its total weight. The historical component therefore responds more slowly to new gradients later in training, suggesting that a separate momentum state emphasizing recent gradients can complement this long-term accumulation.

Building on this perspective, we propose Hybrid Momentum ( HyM ), which combines a linearly weighted gradient average with a geometrically discounted fast momentum. The average assigns weights proportional to the gradients’ iteration indices and retains a growing span of history, while the fast momentum emphasizes recent gradients. HyM also maintains an averaged iterate formed from its training iterates for evaluation and checkpointing. Our convergence analysis via cumulative gradient weights accommodates this growing gradient memory and establishes an 𝒪 ( T − 1 / 2 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2}) bound on the expected suboptimality of the averaged iterate for smooth convex objectives. Moreover, this hybrid momentum scheme is modular and can be combined with adaptive preconditioning and other update transformations. In particular, applying Muon’s Newton–Schulz (NS) orthogonalization to the combined momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , we develop Hybrid Momentum Orthogonalized by NS ( HyMUON ), which applies to matrix-valued parameters.

We characterize the weights assigned to past gradients and use controlled experiments to examine why this history can remain useful. These experiments show that a gradient contribution retained in the optimizer state can still lower a target loss thousands of steps later, and that replacing this contribution with a gradient recomputed on the same batch at the current parameters can lower the loss further. We also examine how gradients from different training examples vary in their usefulness for a given target and how HyM ’s relative performance changes with batch size. Across the evaluated benchmarks, HyM matches or improves upon Schedule-Free on image classification, while HyMUON improves upon Muon on IWSLT14 and across the evaluated language modeling settings. Momentum methods use past information in two standard ways: by accumulating gradients or by introducing inertial terms based on differences between successive iterates ( Polyak, 1964 ; Nesterov, 1983 ) . For smooth convex stochastic optimization, Lan (2012) established an optimal convergence rate for accelerated stochastic approximation; Yang et al. (2016) and Ghadimi and Lan (2016) analyzed stochastic momentum and accelerated gradient methods for smooth nonconvex objectives. More recently, Wang and Yurtsever (2026) unified Polyak and Nesterov variants within a generalized SGDM framework and analyzed both convex and nonconvex smooth objectives. In deep learning, EMA-Nesterov replaces the standard lookahead direction with an exponential moving average of parameter updates, which stabilizes the extrapolation performed by a base optimizer ( Yau et al., 2026 ) .

Several methods combine momentum components to capture different timescales. Aggregated Heavy-Ball studies the convergence of schemes with multiple components ( Danilova, 2022 ) . AdEMAMix pairs two EMAs whose decay coefficients differ by orders of magnitude, so that one retains gradients over short histories and the other over long ones ( Pagliardini et al., 2025 ) . HyM also uses a fast state and a slow state, but replaces the slow EMA with a linearly weighted gradient average. This replacement changes not only the length of the retained history but also the distribution of weight over that history. AdEMAMix raises its slow decay coefficient during warmup and then holds it at a prescribed value; consequently, the fraction of its total gradient weight assigned to the first ⌊ a ​ t ⌋ \lfloor at\rfloor gradients converges to zero for any fixed a ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) a\in(0,1) . For HyM , the corresponding fraction converges to the positive constant β 2 − β ​ a 2 \frac{\beta}{2-\beta}a^{2} .

Morwani et al. (2025) show that Schedule-Free optimization ( Defazio et al., 2024 ) can be expressed as accelerated SGD followed by weight averaging, which separates the roles of gradient memory and the averaged iterate. ScheduleFree+ restores Adam’s inner state for the first moment and extends this construction with Polyak adaptation of the learning rate, delayed averaging, and an annealed interpolation between its raw and averaged iterates ( Defazio, 2026 ) . In ScheduleFree+, the averaged iterate is still fed into the next gradient query; hence, the sequence that will be returned also steers training. HyM separates the two. Its averaged iterate never enters the gradient or the momentum recursion, and the update direction combines the two momentum states alone. The convergence analyses also differ in kind. The Schedule-Free analysis uses an online-to-batch conversion for convex optimization ( Defazio et al., 2024 ) . Ours tracks how a gradient memory that grows with training interacts with iterate averaging, and bounds the averaged iterate directly. Preconditioning is also important for training large language models. Two common approaches are diagonal preconditioning, which scales each coordinate by its own factor as in Adam and AdamW ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , and structured matrix preconditioning, as in Shampoo, K-FAC, and SOAP ( Gupta et al., 2018 ; Martens and Grosse, 2015 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) . More recently, Muon has been used to train large models by applying NS orthogonalization to matrix momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , which motivated subsequent work on efficiency, stability, and distributed training ( Li et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team, 2025 ; Ahn et al., 2025 ) .

chunks.section: 4 Why Past Gradients Can Remain Useful
chunks.text: From Algorithm 1 , we can derive that, for any proportion a ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) a\in(0,1) , the first ⌊ a ​ t ⌋ \lfloor at\rfloor gradients account for a fraction of HyM ’s total gradient weight that converges to β 2 − β ​ a 2 \frac{\beta}{2-\beta}a^{2} , which is positive, as t → ∞ t\to\infty , whereas the corresponding fraction under EMA momentum converges to zero. Thus, compared with EMA momentum, HyM asymptotically retains more weight on older gradients. In this section, we examine why retaining such a long history can be useful. We first characterize how the two states distribute weight over the gradient history. We then test whether a retained gradient can still affect training thousands of steps later. Finally, we examine whether gradients computed from examples in the actual training data differ substantially in their usefulness for a given target.

chunks.section: 4.1 Retaining history while responding to change
chunks.text: HyM combines two momentum states that cover different ranges of the gradient history. The slow state draws on an increasingly long history, whereas the fast state remains concentrated on recent gradients. We quantify this difference using the average lag and then examine the resulting weights in the update direction. At iteration t t , a gradient 𝐠 i \mathbf{g}_{i} computed at iteration i i is t − i t-i iterations old. To summarize the age of the gradients used by a momentum state, we normalize its weights to sum to one and define the average lag as the weighted average of t − i t-i over i = 1 , … , t i=1,\ldots,t . It is ( t − 1 ) / 3 (t-1)/3 for the slow state and converges to μ / ( 1 − μ ) \mu/(1-\mu) for the fast state as t t grows. Hence, the average lag of the slow state increases with t t , whereas that of the fast state remains bounded. chunks.section: 4.2 Old gradients can still affect later steps
chunks.text: To test whether the effect of a single batch persists during subsequent training, we adapt an experiment from AdEMAMix ( Pagliardini et al., 2025 ) to GPT-2 124M trained on OpenWebText. We exclude a fixed batch ℬ \mathcal{B} from the regular training sequence and use its loss to track the lasting effect of a single update. Starting from a common checkpoint immediately before step 5,000, we continue training along two branches. At step 5,000, the control branch uses the batch specified by the original training sequence, whereas the inject branch replaces that batch with ℬ \mathcal{B} . Both branches subsequently use the same sequence of training batches. At step 10,000, the loss on ℬ \mathcal{B} in the control branch exceeds that in the inject branch by approximately 0.030 0.030 for Muon and 0.016 0.016 for HyMUON (Figure 2 , left). Thus, the effect of a single update based on ℬ \mathcal{B} remains measurable after 5,000 subsequent training steps. We next conduct a further experiment by modifying the contribution of ℬ \mathcal{B} retained in the slow state. At step 7,500, we split the inject branch from the preceding experiment into three branches: Keep, Delete, and Refresh. At this point, the contribution introduced at step 5,000 still has weight 5,000 / 7,500 = 2 / 3 5{,}000/7{,}500=2/3 in the slow state. Keep leaves this contribution unchanged, Delete removes it, and Refresh replaces it with a gradient computed on ℬ \mathcal{B} at the current model parameters and rescaled to have the same norm. At step 7,500, the three branches differ only in this contribution to the slow state; their model parameters, averaged iterate 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} , and all other optimizer states are otherwise identical. Appendix E.3.1 gives the precise construction.

chunks.section: 4.3 Useful contributions are uneven across training examples
chunks.text: The preceding experiment deliberately inserts a fixed batch ℬ \mathcal{B} to isolate the persistence of its effect. We next ask whether examples drawn from the training data naturally produce gradients that differ in their usefulness for the same target. In language model pretraining, data are drawn from a distribution that can be divided into several domains. For a particular domain, gradients computed from different training examples may reduce its loss by different amounts. We examine this variation across candidate passages at fixed model parameters. To test this idea, we use groups of semantically related passages as semantic targets, each representing a specific part of the data distribution. We conduct this experiment at three checkpoints of GPT-2 124M and use 2,000 candidate passages from the training data, each containing 256 tokens. For each candidate passage, we restore the model to the same checkpoint, compute the gradient on that passage, normalize the gradient, and take one step with a fixed length. All candidates are therefore compared from the same model parameters, without any influence from optimizer state. We use E5 embeddings ( Wang et al., 2022 ) to construct ten semantic targets from passages in a separate validation set. Each semantic target is divided into a reference set and an evaluation set. We use the same pretrained E5 encoder to measure the semantic similarity between each candidate and the reference set. After taking the candidate’s gradient step, we measure how much this step reduces the loss on the evaluation set. Appendix E.2 provides additional construction details and statistics.

chunks.text: Figure 3 summarizes the results of this experiment. It groups the candidate passages by their E5 similarity to each semantic target and reports the mean improvement within each percentile. At all three checkpoints, the improvement generally increases with similarity and rises particularly sharply among the most similar candidates. Moreover, at each checkpoint, the 20 % 20\% of candidates with the highest similarity account for approximately one third of the positive improvement specific to the corresponding targets. Appendix E.2 provides the precise definition, exact statistics, and results for individual targets. The blue curves show the mean across ten semantic targets, and the shaded regions show error bands across targets. chunks.section: 4.3 Useful contributions are uneven across training examples
chunks.text: The experiment in Figure 2 shows that the effect of a single gradient update can remain measurable thousands of steps later. The experiment in Figure 3 shows that gradient usefulness varies substantially across training passages: at each checkpoint, the candidates with the highest similarity constitute only one fifth of all candidates but account for approximately one third of the positive improvement specific to the corresponding targets. Thus, gradients that are particularly useful for a target are not distributed evenly across training examples. Together, these results support retaining gradients over a long history. When such gradients occur intermittently, retaining their contributions allows subsequent updates to continue using this information when later training examples provide little useful gradient information for that target. The slow state of HyM is designed to retain such contributions effectively in subsequent updates.

In this section, we establish the convergence of HyM for smooth convex objectives. For EMA momentum with a fixed decay factor μ \mu , the average lag approaches the constant μ / ( 1 − μ ) \mu/(1-\mu) . Therefore, the average age of the gradients remains bounded as training proceeds. In contrast, the slow state of HyM has average lag ( t − 1 ) / 3 (t-1)/3 , which grows with t t . Appendix F gives the complete configurations and evaluation protocols, and Table 1 summarizes the numerical results. CIFAR and SVHN use their test splits, IWSLT reports test metrics, and ImageNet uses its official validation split. The vision and IWSLT curves show means across repeated runs, and the shaded regions show one standard error. The values in the vision panel legends are endpoint means with sample standard deviations. We compare HyM with momentum SGD using cosine or step schedules for the learning rate and with Schedule-Free SGD on CIFAR-10 (WRN-16-8), CIFAR-100 (DenseNet-BC), SVHN (ResNet-3-96), and ImageNet-1K (ResNet-50) ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ; Netzer et al., 2011 ; Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) . HyM is evaluated at its averaged iterate, as described in Appendix F . HyM reaches mean test accuracy of 96.25 % 96.25\% on CIFAR-10 and 98.47 % 98.47\% on SVHN, compared with 96.11 % 96.11\% for Schedule-Free SGD on CIFAR-10 and 98.24 % 98.24\% for cosine SGD on SVHN (Table 1 ). On CIFAR-100, the mean test accuracies are 79.14 % 79.14\% for HyM and 79.11 % 79.11\% for Schedule-Free SGD. ImageNet mean validation top-1 accuracies are 76.84 % 76.84\% for HyM , 76.70 % 76.70\% for Schedule-Free SGD, and 76.68 % 76.68\% for cosine SGD. Schedule-Free SGD has higher validation accuracy during early training on ImageNet, while its curve and that of HyM become close later in training (Figure 4 , right panels).

On IWSLT14 German–English ( Cettolo et al., 2014 ) , we train Fairseq’s LSTM preset with attention ( Ott et al., 2019 ) for 55 epochs. We tune each optimizer separately and evaluate the selected configurations over repeated runs. At each epoch, the reported test metrics come from the checkpoint with the highest validation BLEU observed up to that epoch. Averaged over runs, HyMUON reaches test loss 4.184 ± 0.004 4.184\pm 0.004 and BLEU 33.874 ± 0.072 33.874\pm 0.072 , against 4.234 ± 0.006 4.234\pm 0.006 and 33.424 ± 0.048 33.424\pm 0.048 for Muon, where the values are means with sample standard deviations (Table 1 ; Figure 5 , top left; Figure 14 in Appendix F.4 ).

We pretrain GPT-2 124M ( Radford et al., 2019 ) from scratch on OpenWebText ( Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019 ) in two separate experiments, one for 100k steps and the other for 600k steps. HyMUON reaches final validation losses of 2.886 2.886 and 2.823 2.823 , respectively, lower than AdamW and Muon at both training lengths (Figure 5 , top middle and bottom left; full results in Table 1 ).

chunks.text: We compare AdamW, AdEMAMix, Muon, and HyMUON using the same FineWeb subset and the 124M protocol for large batches from Semenov et al. (2025) , with separate runs using 1B and 2.1B tokens. At 1B tokens, HyMUON reaches final validation loss 3.47 3.47 , compared with 3.48 3.48 for AdEMAMix. At 2.1B tokens, HyMUON and AdEMAMix both have validation loss 3.35 3.35 after rounding to two decimal places, while Muon and AdamW both have 3.39 3.39 (Figure 5 , bottom middle and bottom right). Protocol details are in Appendix F.7 .

We compare HyMUON against Muon reproduced with the hyperparameters selected by Gu and Xie (2026) for LLaMA-1.3B/C4. We tune the HyMUON optimizer hyperparameters; Appendix F.6 gives the selected configuration. Training uses C4/en with document packing for 10k steps. HyMUON reaches validation loss 2.777 2.777 , compared with 2.903 2.903 for Muon (Figure 5 , top right). The corresponding perplexity curves are reported in Figure 16 in Appendix F.6 . Appendix G reports an additional evaluation of HyMUON on the modded-nanoGPT Track 3 benchmark.

EMA momentum reduces a gradient’s weight geometrically according to the number of iterations that have passed since the gradient was computed. The controlled experiments show that a gradient contribution retained in the optimizer state can still reduce a target loss thousands of steps later and that gradients computed from different training examples can make substantially different contributions to the same loss. HyM separates long-term retention from short-term adaptation by using a slow state that draws on a growing gradient history and a fast state that emphasizes recent gradients. For smooth convex objectives, HyM achieves an 𝒪 ( T − 1 / 2 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2}) bound at its final averaged iterate, while HyM and HyMUON match or improve upon the baselines considered across image classification, machine translation, and language modeling. The broader lesson is that the age of a gradient need not determine its usefulness. Momentum need not serve only as a short-term smoother; it can also provide long-term memory for useful gradient information that appears intermittently during training.

chunks.section: B.4.1 Rosenbrock illustration and the role of the averaged iterate
chunks.text: The preceding subsections analyze how the two momentum states distribute weight over the gradient history and respond to changes in the gradient mean. We now turn to a separate component of HyM : the averaged iterate. The following example illustrates how averaging the training iterates interacts with motion along a curved valley. Consider gradients whose dominant component changes sign across iterations while a smaller component remains consistently aligned. Averaging attenuates the component whose sign varies relative to the consistently aligned component. For the Rosenbrock function f RB f_{\rm RB} defined below, the component of ∇ f RB \nabla f_{\rm RB} normal to the curve v = u 2 v=u^{2} changes sign across iterates, while the tangential component can retain its sign. This geometric motivation also appears in AdEMAMix and Schedule-Free analyses [ Pagliardini et al., 2025 , Song et al., 2025 ] . The slow state averages gradients over the trajectory, allowing normal components that change sign to cancel while tangential components that retain their sign accumulate. The fast state places greater weight on gradients computed near the current part of the valley. The two states therefore capture complementary parts of the gradient history. We visualize this behavior on f RB ​ ( u , v ) = ( 1 − u ) 2 + 100 ​ ( v − u 2 ) 2 f_{\rm RB}(u,v)=(1-u)^{2}+100(v-u^{2})^{2} . chunks.section: E.1 Dependence of the HyM advantage on batch size
chunks.text: Because the variance of a mini-batch gradient generally increases as the batch size decreases, we examine how the relative performance of HyM varies with batch size. We use CIFAR-10 with WideResNet-16-8 and CIFAR-100 with DenseNet-BC, training each model for 300 epochs on its full training set. We use B ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 , 128 , 256 , 1024 , 2048 } B\in\{8,16,32,128,256,1024,2048\} on CIFAR-10 and B ∈ { 64,128,256,512 , 1024 } B\in\{64,128,256,512,1024\} on CIFAR-100. Within each dataset, the model, augmentation, and optimizer settings other than the learning rate are fixed across batch sizes as in Appendix F.1 ; both methods use a 5% warmup followed by cosine decay, ending at half the peak learning rate for HyM and zero for SGD. Peak learning rates use candidates specific to each method and batch size, obtained by linear scaling with batch size. Figure 8 reports test loss for the selected configuration of each method and batch size. Figure 8: Test loss against training batch size on CIFAR-10 (left) and CIFAR-100 (right). The learning rate is chosen separately for each method and batch size. HyM has lower observed test loss at every plotted batch size. On CIFAR-10, the gap narrows from about 0.042 0.042 at B = 8 B=8 to 0.001 0.001 at B = 2048 B=2048 as the batch size increases. On CIFAR-100, the gap is about 0.261 0.261 at B = 64 B=64 and 0.205 0.205 at B = 1024 B=1024 , but does not vary monotonically across the intervening batch sizes.

Section 4.3 uses GPT-2 124M checkpoints at 10k, 50k, and 100k steps of an AdamW run initialized from public GPT-2 weights and continued on OpenWebText. Each step processes 491,520 tokens. AdamW uses ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) , weight decay 0.1 0.1 , a warmup over 2k steps to 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} , and cosine decay to 6 × 10 − 5 6\times 10^{-5} at 100k. The experiment loads model parameters only. Its 2,000 candidates are uniformly sampled training passages containing 256 tokens and lying within document boundaries. They are screened to exclude passages that are nearly duplicates of the target texts.

A fixed pretrained intfloat/e5-small-v2 encoder [ Wang et al., 2022 ] embeds 16,384 validation passages, with a passage: prefix and masked mean pooling. We subtract the embedding mean and its first three principal components estimated on 4,096 background training passages, then normalize each embedding. MiniBatchKMeans partitions the embeddings into 128 clusters. We select ten clusters and take 64 passages from distinct documents in each cluster, dividing them evenly into 32 reference and 32 evaluation passages. Ten controls each mix 64 randomly chosen passages from other documents and use the same split. All passages contain 256 tokens. These targets are defined by the encoder rather than by annotated grammatical or factual categories. Semantic similarity is computed solely from the reference passages, whereas loss reduction is evaluated solely on the evaluation passages. For a candidate’s embedding, its E5 score is the mean of its maximum and mean cosine similarity to the 32 reference embeddings. We also regress this score on two measures of lexical overlap within each target: the cosine similarity between vectors of token frequencies weighted by inverse document frequency, and the cosine similarity between vectors of bigram frequencies after centering with background statistics. The residual measures the part not linearly explained by these two measures. Gradient cosine similarity compares the candidate gradient with the gradient computed on the reference set at the same checkpoint.

chunks.section: E.3.1 Intervention on the slow momentum state
chunks.text: The right panel of Figure 2 continues the injection protocol with an intervention on the slow state at step 7,500. Let 𝐠 ℬ ​ ( s ) \mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{B}}(s) and 𝐠 ℛ ​ ( s ) \mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{R}}(s) denote the gradients at the common parameters at step s s on ℬ \mathcal{B} and on the batch ℛ \mathcal{R} from the original training sequence, respectively. Because the inject branch replaces ℛ \mathcal{R} with ℬ \mathcal{B} at step s = 5,000 s=5{,}000 , the contribution introduced into its slow state is the signed difference Δ ​ 𝐠 s = 𝐠 ℬ ​ ( s ) − 𝐠 ℛ ​ ( s ) \Delta\mathbf{g}_{s}=\mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{B}}(s)-\mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{R}}(s) rather than 𝐠 ℬ ​ ( s ) \mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{B}}(s) alone. In HyMUON ’s slow state, a gradient from step s s has coefficient s / t s/t at step t t ; consequently, the coefficient of Δ ​ 𝐠 s \Delta\mathbf{g}_{s} is 2 / 3 2/3 at the intervention. The Delete branch subtracts this exact contribution from the slow states of the matrix and auxiliary parameter groups. The Refresh branch first performs the same deletion and then computes 𝐠 ℬ ​ ( 7,500 ) \mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{B}}(7{,}500) at the current training iterate, rescaling its matrix and auxiliary components separately to match the norm of the corresponding removed component within each parameter group.

chunks.section: E.3.1 Intervention on the slow momentum state
chunks.text: Immediately before the intervention, Keep, Delete, and Refresh are initialized from identical copies of the inject branch. These copies include the model parameters and buffers, all optimizer states including the averaged iterate 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} , the scheduler for the learning rate, the training counters, and the states of the random number generators and data samplers on every rank. The three interventions are then applied to these copies, followed by the same sequence of training batches. The gradient computation required by Refresh preserves the random states and model buffers used for subsequent training. At the same lag, the corresponding coefficients of the matrix momentum and auxiliary first moment for Muon are approximately 2.0 × 10 − 56 2.0\times 10^{-56} and 4.0 × 10 − 116 4.0\times 10^{-116} . Both are numerically negligible at this lag; hence, the intervention isolates HyMUON ’s persistent slow state rather than Muon’s memory. The intervention does not modify model parameters, the averaged iterate 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} , the fast state, or either state for the second moment. Immediately before the next step in the common training sequence, the code applies the complete NS or adaptive transformation to the original and intervened states. After multiplication by the learning rate, the differences between the resulting parameter updates have norms 0.104 0.104 for Delete and 0.111 0.111 for Refresh. At step 10,000, the losses on ℬ \mathcal{B} are 3.047617 3.047617 for Delete, 3.038296 3.038296 for Keep, and 3.025494 3.025494 for Refresh.

chunks.section: F.3 Component ablation of HyM on CIFAR-10
chunks.text: We compare the fast momentum, slow momentum, their combination, and three replacements of the slow momentum by an EMA with a fixed decay rate. Each training trajectory is evaluated at both the training iterate 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and the averaged iterate 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , which allows the effect of iterate averaging to be separated from the choice of gradient history.

We train WideResNet-16-8 for 300 epochs on a fixed split stratified by class of CIFAR-10: 45,000 training images and 5,000 validation images, with 500 validation images per class. Batch size is 128 without dropping the final batch, giving 352 steps per epoch and T = 105,600 T=105{,}600 steps in total. The three peak learning rates η max ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 } \eta_{\max}\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\} define separate comparison groups, all of which are reported. To distinguish the two roles of the mixing weight in this ablation, we denote the direction and averaging weights by β dir \beta_{\mathrm{dir}} and β avg \beta_{\mathrm{avg}} , respectively; both are set to 0.95 0.95 . All groups use μ = 0.99 \mu=0.99 and coupled L2 decay λ wd = 5 × 10 − 4 \lambda_{\mathrm{wd}}=5\times 10^{-4} on all parameters. The learning rate warms up linearly for 5,280 steps, then follows a cosine decay to η max / 2 \eta_{\max}/2 . Training uses cross-entropy, deterministic cuDNN, and no cuDNN benchmarking. Augmentation is a random 32 × 32 32\times 32 crop after reflection padding of four pixels and a horizontal flip with probability 0.5 0.5 ; each channel is normalized as ( pixel / 255 − 0.5 ) / 0.5 (\mathrm{pixel}/255-0.5)/0.5 . Initialization, the order of training images, and the randomness in cropping and flipping are shared across configurations. After every epoch, 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and 𝐱 \mathbf{x} are copied in turn into a separate evaluation model. For each evaluated iterate, Batch Normalization statistics are reset and recalibrated by cumulative averaging on the same 6,400 unaugmented training images (50 batches). Neither parameters nor BN buffers are copied back into the training model. We report epoch-300 validation metrics.
